items.prompt: What is a manager's unit of output?
choices: The output of the people they manage
Their own number of merged PRs
The total hours they personally work each week
items.explanation: The job's output moved from your own work to the team's work.

items.prompt: Maya's PRs went from 12 to 15 a month. What does that number measure?
choices: How well her whole team is doing now
How good a manager she has become
Her own output only
items.explanation: Her PR count is the old IC scoreboard; it says nothing about the team.

items.prompt: Which phrase describes the leverage of a manager's role?
choices: A multiplier of one
A stand-in
A multiplier of many people
items.explanation: A manager's effect runs through the team's collective effort.

items.prompt: Which is a sign Maya's team is not well supported?
choices: Maya merged 15 PRs this month
Two of four reports are unclear on priority
The team has only four members in total, no more
items.explanation: Unclear priorities directly reduce each person's effective output.

items.prompt: Compared with an IC, what does the manager equation add?
choices: How many hours the manager spends coding
Each person's support
How fast the manager can type code
items.explanation: Support (clarity, context, unblocking) multiplies every person's output.

items.prompt: Maya's release cadence halved after the promotion. Which scoreboard shows it?
choices: The team's output
Her personal PR count alone
Her calendar
items.explanation: Cadence is a team result; her PR count would never reveal it.

items.prompt: True or false: a manager who is the top personal producer is doing the job well.
choices: False; personal output alone does not show it
True, producing is the job
True, if quality is high
items.explanation: Personal output and team output are different measures.

items.prompt: Why did Maya's own number go up after the promotion?
choices: Her team asked her to code more
Management training made her much faster at coding
She kept doing the work she knows best
items.explanation: She is optimizing the old equation, not the new one.

items.prompt: Maya's PRs rose from 12 to 15 while two of four reports lost sight of priorities. Which reading of those two facts is correct?
choices: Her output rose, so the priority confusion is the reports' own fault
Her own term rose while terms she now owns fell
Both are individual results and cannot be compared at all
Her rising output proves the team is slightly better supported
items.explanation: The manager equation sums across the team; her PRs are one old term, and the unsupported reports are the cost on the new ones.
items.reference:
Whose output counts
IC: your own work
Manager: the team's work
Maya: PRs up, team clarity down
Why: a manager's job output is the team's work, so personal output can rise while the real scoreboard falls.
items.learnMore:
A manager's real output

A manager's output is the output of the people they manage, so the scoreboard changes when the job does.

Common mistake

Judging a manager by their own merged PRs, because that is easy to count.
items.reflection: Think of a role you held where the thing you were measured on changed. Did you notice the change, or keep optimizing the old measure?

items.prompt: A director praises a manager for closing more tickets than anyone on the team. What is the strongest objection?
choices: Ticket count is an IC measure, not the team's output
Closing tickets takes time away from attending leadership meetings
Ticket counts are always easier to manipulate than other numbers
Managers should close tickets only when the team asks them to
items.explanation: The objection is about the scoreboard: personal output is not what the manager role produces.

items.prompt: Two managers each work 50 hours. One's team grows clearer and faster; the other's stays unclear. What best explains the gap?
choices: The first manager simply has a more talented set of reports
The second manager must have worked more slowly
Hours worked decides the team's output regardless of where those hours are actually spent
How the hours were split between enabling others and doing their own work
items.explanation: Equal effort can land on different terms of the equation; enabling work is what lifts the team.

items.prompt: What is the retreat trap?
choices: Leaving the company soon after a promotion
Refusing to delegate any technical decision at all
Falling back to familiar hands-on work
items.explanation: It is the pull back to what you already do well.

items.prompt: Why does a new manager retreat to coding?
choices: Managers are not allowed to coach anyone
It is familiar and gives fast feedback
Code is always the most urgent thing on the list
items.explanation: Familiarity and quick results make it the easy default.

items.prompt: Is the code a retreating manager writes usually bad?
choices: Yes, it is usually sloppy
No, it is often excellent, which hides the problem
It is rarely finished
items.explanation: That is what makes the trap hard to notice.

items.prompt: Which task can only the manager do?
choices: Setting priorities across other teams
Writing the tricky module for this sprint's release
Fixing a small bug in a service
items.explanation: Context, authority and relationships sit with the manager.

items.prompt: What does retreating cost the team?
choices: Coaching, unblocking and clear priorities
Faster reviews on every PR
A bigger pile of finished tickets that nobody asked for
items.explanation: The manager's unique contributions go missing.

items.prompt: How does an unfamiliar management task usually feel?
choices: Easy and instantly rewarding to complete
The same as writing code
Slow and uncomfortable
items.explanation: That discomfort is what drives the retreat.

items.prompt: Who could plausibly write the tricky module instead of the manager?
choices: Nobody else at the whole company
Only the newest hire
A strong engineer on the team
items.explanation: Hands-on work usually has other capable owners; the manager role does not.

items.prompt: Is retreating a sign the manager is lazy?
choices: Yes, it is always laziness
No; it usually reflects discomfort, not laziness
Yes, it means they dislike the team
items.explanation: Retreaters often work harder than ever, as Maya does.

items.prompt: A new manager spends most of the week on a tricky module because it is the quickest way to feel useful. What is the main problem?
choices: The module will probably be of lower quality than before
The manager is breaking a firm company rule against any hands-on work by managers
The week went to work others could do while manager-only work waited
The team will resent seeing the manager write code
items.explanation: The cost is the opportunity: only the manager can set priorities or coach; the code has other owners.
items.reference:
Unfamiliar vs. familiar tasks
Set priority across teams: only the manager
Coach a stuck report: mostly the manager
Write the module: someone else could
Why: the familiar task is productive and comfortable, which is exactly why it quietly crowds out the work only the manager can do.
items.learnMore:
The retreat trap

Retreating to familiar hands-on work feels productive, but it withholds capacity the team cannot get elsewhere.

Common mistake

Assuming that because the code is good, the week was well spent.
items.reflection: Where do you reach for the comfortable, familiar task when the unclear one is the one that actually matters?

items.prompt: Which scenario is the retreat trap rather than healthy hands-on work?
choices: Writing one small fix during a rare outage with the team away
Taking the hardest bug to dodge a feedback talk
Reviewing a design doc the team lead asked them to read
Pairing briefly to show how the codebase is organized
items.explanation: The tell is the motive: choosing familiar work to avoid an uncomfortable manager task.

items.prompt: Why does the pull recur even for a manager who understands the trap?
choices: Every new ambiguity brings back the comfort of familiar work
Understanding it makes hands-on work more enjoyable than the manager role itself
Experienced managers are expected to prefer technical tasks
It only disappears after changing teams or employers
items.explanation: The discomfort that drives it returns whenever the situation is unclear again.

items.prompt: Does being an excellent IC automatically make you a good manager?
choices: Yes, because strong ICs always learn fast
No, the skills are different
Only on technical teams
items.explanation: The two jobs need different skills that share a career ladder.

items.prompt: Which manager skill matches 'solving a hard problem yourself'?
choices: Letting someone struggle productively
Solving it faster than before
Hiding the problem from the whole team for a while
items.explanation: Jumping in works against building the other person's skill.

items.prompt: Which manager skill matches 'writing clear code'?
choices: Writing clear, usable feedback
Writing longer code comments throughout the repo
Writing more detailed design documents
items.explanation: Feedback has to land without demotivating.

items.prompt: Prioritizing the team's work differs from prioritizing your own because it...
choices: Has fewer items to rank
Needs no judgment
Spans several people's conflicting work
items.explanation: It needs visibility across other people's work.

items.prompt: Which IC habit can work against a manager's team?
choices: Writing readable code
Checking work twice before sharing it
Proving competence by always being right
items.explanation: Reports need to feel safe to disagree.

items.prompt: Is management harder or better than being an IC?
choices: Harder, always
Neither; it is a different job
Better, in every case and on every team
items.explanation: They are different jobs, not a ranking.

items.prompt: Why is treating promotion as just a reward risky?
choices: It makes raises too small
It ignores that the job changed
It delays the next promotion by a year or more
items.explanation: The new manager and team get set up for a rough transition.

items.prompt: What should a new manager do about the skills gap?
choices: Deliberately build the new skills
Hope technical skill carries over on its own
Avoid the new tasks
items.explanation: Coaching, delegating and prioritizing have to be learned on purpose.

items.prompt: A strong engineer, now a manager, rewrites a teammate's pull request instead of commenting. Which cost is specific to the new job?
choices: The pull request merges a few hours later than it should
The rewritten version is slightly harder for others to follow
The manager has less time left for their own deadlines
The teammate never builds the skill, so the mistake returns
items.explanation: The cost is to the team's capability, which is what the manager is now responsible for.
items.reference:
IC skill vs. manager skill
Solve it yourself vs. let them struggle
Clear code vs. clear feedback
Own backlog vs. team-wide priorities
Being right vs. safe to disagree
Why: each IC strength has a manager counterpart that is a separate skill, and the IC instinct can work against it.
items.learnMore:
Skills that do not transfer 1:1

Excellence at the work and excellence at enabling others are different competencies that share a ladder.

Common mistake

Assuming a strong IC will be a strong manager automatically.
items.reflection: Pick a skill you are strong at. What is the related skill needed to help someone else do it, and have you practiced that one?

items.prompt: Which pairing correctly matches an IC skill with the different muscle a manager needs?
choices: Writing fast code versus delivering slower code with more care
Reviewing code versus reviewing budgets in the leadership meeting
Being right in the room versus making it safe for reports to disagree
Debugging alone versus debugging faster in pairs with a peer
items.explanation: The IC habit of showing competence by having the answer can suppress the dissent a manager needs.

Top engineers prefer to stay on a technical path forever
Promotion should only follow a long trial period

items.prompt: Which weekly question fits a manager's scoreboard?
choices: Is my team more capable and clear than a month ago?
What did I personally ship this week?
How many hours of meetings and 1:1s did I attend this week?
items.explanation: The question has to be about the team's output.

items.prompt: Why is the right question easy to replace with the wrong one?
choices: It has no real answer at all
It matters less than the personal one
It is slower and harder to answer
items.explanation: Fast, familiar feedback wins by default.

items.prompt: In this unit's demo model, what does a team of 4 gain at 0 enabling hours?
choices: 37 extra team hours
61 extra team hours per week
Nothing extra
items.explanation: The model gives 0 when the manager spends no time enabling.

items.prompt: In the demo model, the first few enabling hours buy...
choices: The least output
The most output of any hours
No output whatsoever
items.explanation: Returns diminish: clearing obvious blockers matters most.

items.prompt: In the model, a team of 4 at 15 enabling hours gains about...
choices: 9 team hours
37 team hours per week
74 team hours
items.explanation: The demo's default for 4 people at 15 hours rounds to 37.

items.prompt: In the model, going from 35 to 40 enabling hours adds about...
choices: 4 team hours
21 team hours
40 team hours
items.explanation: The curve flattens: 57 rises only to 61.

items.prompt: Does the demo model say a manager should enable 40 hours and never do hands-on work?
choices: No; it shows diminishing returns
Yes, maximize enabling
Yes, because it ignores the cost of lost hands-on work
items.explanation: It is a teaching model about the shape of the trade-off.

items.prompt: In the model, adding people to the team (same enabling hours) generally...
choices: Lowers it to zero
Leaves it exactly unchanged
Raises the total team gain
items.explanation: Total gain scales with team size in the model.

items.prompt: In this unit's demo model, a team of 4 gets about 21 extra hours from the first 5 enabling hours and about 4 from the last 5. What is the takeaway?
choices: Make sure the early, high-return enabling hours happen first
Spend as few hours as possible on enabling work
Never exceed the point where returns begin to shrink
Spread enabling hours evenly across every working day
items.explanation: Diminishing returns mean the first hours, clearing obvious blockers, matter most.
items.reference:
Modeled team output by enabling hours (team of 4)
5 hrs enabling: about 21 team hrs
15 hrs: about 37
40 hrs: about 61
Why: the first enabling hours buy the most, so the right question is whether the team is more capable and clear, not what you personally produced.
items.learnMore:
Measuring the right output

Ask whether the team is more capable, unblocked and clear than a month ago; in this unit's demo model, early enabling hours buy the most.

Common mistake

Swapping the hard team-level question for the easy personal-output one.
items.reflection: What is one question you could ask yourself weekly that measures your team's progress rather than your own output?

items.prompt: In Path A, what does the manager do in Week 1?
choices: Runs a kickoff for the team
Sets a ranked priority list for everyone
Writes the design doc personally
items.explanation: Path A retreats to the familiar task of authoring the doc.

items.prompt: In Path B, who writes the design doc?
choices: The manager alone, with the team reviewing it afterward
An experienced engineer, coached by the manager
Nobody
items.explanation: The manager reviews and coaches instead of authoring.

items.prompt: In Week 2, Path A fixes the stuck engineer's bug...
choices: By pairing for several days
Directly, in about twenty minutes
By asking the engineer to try again for a few days
items.explanation: Fast today, but the underlying gap stays open.

items.prompt: In Week 2, what does Path B do instead?
choices: Asks questions so the engineer finds the fix
Supplies the answer after watching them struggle briefly
Reassigns the engineer to a different team
items.explanation: It is slower this week but closes the gap.

items.prompt: Why does Path B's manager hold the cross-team priority conversations?
choices: Only the manager has the standing for them
The team cannot talk to other teams
They simply prefer meetings
items.explanation: Those conversations depend on the manager's authority and context.

items.prompt: By Week 4, whose stuck engineer has solved two similar problems alone?
choices: Path A's
Both of their engineers
Path B's
items.explanation: Path B's coaching closed the gap; Path A's repeated the quick fix.

items.prompt: Which statement matches the case?
choices: Path A's manager was lazy
Path B's manager was more talented, and that explains it
Both managers were equally skilled and hardworking
items.explanation: The difference is where their time went.

items.prompt: Who has the lower personal output in Path B?
choices: The team
The manager, as expected
Nobody does
items.explanation: Path B's manager wrote less code, and that is expected.

items.prompt: Why does Path A's month look better on an activity log than Path B's?
choices: Path B's manager did less total work across the whole month
Personal output is visible; team gains show up as the team's
Path A's manager collaborated with the team much more often
Activity logs reward managers who spend more time in meetings
items.explanation: Path A shows a doc and shipped code; Path B's results show up in the team's capability.
items.reference:
Same start, different weeks
Path A: doc, quick fix, more backlog
Path B: kickoff, coaching, priority list
Week 4: A's team flat, B's team up
Why: equal skill and effort can yield different outcomes depending on which problems the manager treats as theirs to enable others to solve.
items.learnMore:
Path A vs. Path B over a month

Both managers are skilled and hardworking; the difference is whether problems are solved directly or enabled, which only shows in the month's trajectory.

Common mistake

Comparing weeks by the manager's personal output, which rates Path A higher every time.
items.reflection: Recall a stretch where you solved something yourself that someone else could have been coached through. What would the other path have cost and bought?

items.prompt: In Week 2, Path A's fix took twenty minutes and Path B's coaching took longer. What does Path B's extra time buy?

A better documented bug fix that others can use later
More time for the stuck engineer to rest between tasks
A guarantee that no similar bugs will ever be introduced
items.explanation: Coaching closes the underlying skill gap; the quick fix only clears one instance.

items.prompt: Is the retreat pull a one-time first-month problem?
choices: Yes, it ends after month one
No, it recurs
Only at large companies
items.explanation: New ambiguity re-creates the comfort gap.

items.prompt: Should a manager never do hands-on technical work again?
choices: No; a total ban is an over-correction
Yes, never again
Yes, after the first year in the role
items.explanation: The shift is in the default, not an absolute rule.

items.prompt: Why might a manager keep some technical touch?
choices: To keep credibility and judgment
To compete with the team
To skip their 1:1s with each report
items.explanation: A fully disconnected manager can lose both.

items.prompt: What is the shift in default behavior under ambiguity?
choices: Code first
Wait and see for a few weeks first
Delegate and coach first
items.explanation: That default fills most of the time without banning all hands-on work.

items.prompt: Judging a new manager by personal output is...
choices: The fairest approach available to leadership
Impossible
Applying the IC standard to a different job
items.explanation: It makes Path B look weaker than Path A.

items.prompt: Promoting someone as a reward, with no new-job framing, sets them up to...
choices: Quit the same week
Struggle with skills nobody taught them
Earn a larger bonus than their former peers
items.explanation: The new skills were never built before the role began.

items.prompt: A manager who followed Path B for a year says the trap is behind them. That is...
choices: Proven true by a full year of good results
Premature, since the pull can return
Irrelevant to anyone else
items.explanation: It is a standing discipline.

items.prompt: Which situation can bring the retreat pull back?
choices: A new team or an unfamiliar conflict
A quiet, predictable week
A finished project that shipped on time
items.explanation: Fresh uncertainty brings back the comfort of familiar work.

items.prompt: After a year on Path B, a manager faces a politically tense new team and starts writing code again. What is this best called?
choices: Proof that the Path B habits never actually worked well
A sensible return to being the team's best contributor
The standing retreat pull resurfacing under new ambiguity
An ordinary sign the manager has outgrown the role
items.explanation: The pull recurs with each fresh uncertainty, however long ago it was resisted.
items.reference:
Traps after month one
Judging by IC standards
Over-correcting to zero hands-on
Treating the retreat as one-time
Promotion as pure reward
Why: the retreat pull recurs under every new ambiguity, so it needs standing discipline, and the fix is a changed default rather than a ban.
items.learnMore:
Failure modes that persist

The retreat is a recurring pull, not a first-month slip; the answer is delegating and coaching first by default, not never touching the work.

Common mistake

Declaring the problem solved after one good month.

Being asked to take on a second team right away
items.explanation: The failure mode is losing touch, not doing too much enabling.
